<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par111 />{{GHGmargin-letter|111|i}}
'''3.''' The {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} serves, in the cases treated under ''a–h'', to represent either expressly, or at least to a great extent, a ''chronological'' succession of actions or events; elsewhere it expresses those actions, &c., which represent the logical consequence of what preceded, or a result arising from it by an inherent necessity. Thus the {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} is used—

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|k}}
(''a'') As a final summing up of the preceding narrative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=20|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּ֫קָם הַשָּׂדֶה וג׳|translate=so}} (in this way) ''the field became'' (legally) ''the property of Abraham'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=50}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=31|verse=6|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|l}}
(''b'') To express a logical or necessary consequence of that which immediately precedes, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=2|verse=3}} ''and he still holdeth fast his integrity'', {{GHGheb|text=וַתְּסִיתֵ֫נִי וג׳|translate=so that thou thus}} (as it now appears) ''groundlessly movedst me against him''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=65|verse=9}} ''so that they are afraid'' ...; even a consequence which happens conditionally, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=וַתְּהִי|translate=so that my mother should have been}} ... Another instance of the kind perhaps (if the text be correct) is {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּ֫מָת|translate=so that he dies}} (must die).

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|m}}
Rem. Such consecutive clauses frequently occur after interrogative sentences, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=51|verse=12}} ''who art thou'' (i.e. art thou ''so helpless''), {{GHGheb|text=וַתִּֽירְאִי|translate=that thou art}} (''must needs be'') ''afraid''? {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=144|verse=3}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=8|verse=5}}, where in a very similar context {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=that}} is used with the imperfect); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=19}} ({{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֶקַּח}}); 31:27 {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֲשַׁלֵּֽחֲךָ|translate=so that I might have sent thee away}}.

'''4.''' As regards the range of time it is to be carefully noticed—

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|n}}
(''a'') That the {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} may represent all varieties in the relations of tense and mood, which, according to {{GHGpar|107|a}}, follow from the idea of the imperfect;

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|o}}
(''b'') That the more precise determination of the range of time to which an {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} relates must be inferred in each case from the character of the preceding tense (or tense-equivalent), to which it is attached, in a more or less close relation, as temporal or logical sequence. Thus the {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} serves—

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|p}}
(1) To represent actions, events, or states, which are ''past'' (or were repeated in past time), when it is united with tenses, or their equivalents, which refer to an actual past.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|q}}
Cf. the examples given above, under ''a'' and ''f'', of the imperfect consecutive as an historic tense. The imperfect consecutive also frequently occurs as the continuation of a perfect (''preterite'') in a subordinate clause; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=37}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=8|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=11|verse=33|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, &c.; also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּבְחָרֶ֫ךָּ}} is the continuation of a preterite, contained, according to the sense, in the preceding {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר נֶֽאֱמָן}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=26}}, 34 the imperfect consecutive is joined to an imperfect denoting the past in a conditional sentence. An imperfect consecutive occurs in dependence on a perfect which has the sense of a pluperfect ({{GHGpar|106|f}}), e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=6|hidebook=1}}f., 31:19, 34 (''now Rachel had taken the teraphim'', {{GHGheb|text=וַתְּשִׂמֵם|translate=and had }}<section end=par111 /><noinclude>
